question.prompt: Suppose \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), differentiable on adjacent intervals \((c-\delta,c)\) and \((c,c+\delta)\) for some \(\delta>0\), and satisfies \(f'(x)>0\) on the left interval and \(f'(x)<0\) on the right interval. What kind of point is \(c\)?

solutions.explanation: The derivative signs make \(f\) strictly increasing to the left of \(c\) and strictly decreasing to its right. Continuity at \(c\) joins these behaviors to the value \(f(c)\). Hence nearby values on both sides are smaller than \(f(c)\), so \(c\) is a local maximum point, C.
solutions.title: Derivative signs and continuity
